utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-05-88-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I'll turn to the accused, one by one. Mr. Popovic, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Beara, the same question. THE ACCUSED BEARA: [Interpretation] I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Drago Nikolic, are you receiving interpretation in your own language? THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, same question. THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Miletic is not here; Gvero is not here. Mr. Pandurevic? THE ACCUSED PANDUREVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, I can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Trbic? THE ACCUSED TRBIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with appearances. I see that Mr. McCloskey is not with us today, and he has justification for that. So, appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Nelson Thayer for the Prosecutor. Beside me is Ms. Lise-Lotte Karlsson, assistant case manager, Lada Soljan, associate legal officer, and behind me are Diana Mautner Marlchof and Christopher Mitchell of our legal staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances will go according to the same order I followed before. Appearances for Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Zoran Zivanovic, counsel for Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. For the accused Beara?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honour. John Ostojic on behalf of Mr. Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Jelena Nikolic and Stephane Bourgon for Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you both. Appearances for Ljubomir Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Counsel Aleksandar Lazarevic for Ljubomir Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Are you on your own today, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Appearances for Radivoje Miletic? MS. FAUVEAU IVANOVIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Natacha Fauveau Ivanovic, and I am the council for Radovan Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam. Appearances for Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Peter Haynes and Djordje Sarapa for Mr. Pandurevic. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you both. For the accused Trbic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROHAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Colleen Rohan appearing for Milorad Trbic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning to everyone, and I welcome you all to this Status Conference, which you will have noticed has been convened much earlier than it would normally have been convened had we not planned already to have -- to start the trial very shortly. And this is a first Status Conference that is being convened at a short interval after the previous one. And there will be others, I think, between now and when the trial starts. We need to discuss several matters. Some would probably be discussed in Status Conferences like this. Others may be discussed with me, alone or with the other two judges in camera, because they may be rather administrative matters in preparation for the trial. Or they could also be -- there could also be meetings with my Senior Legal Officer. As you will recall, the last Status Conference was convened on the 4th of April. And as I have just hinted, because we are planning to start the trial sometime this summer, I thought it was necessary to have a Status Conference earlier; that's today. You are fully aware, and I need barely repeat, that the purpose of a status conference is to organise exchanges between the parties with a view to ensuring an expeditious preparation for trial, and also to give each and every one of the accused the opportunity to meet face to face with me and an opportunity to give you -- that you have to air any grievances or any matter that you would like to bring to my attention. Some days ago, I instructed my SLO to organise a 65 ter meeting with counsel for Prosecution and Defence. This was held yesterday. I am informed that by my SLO that it was a very straightforward and productive 65 ter meeting, and I take this opportunity to thank each and every one of you for making this possible, which makes, then, progress possible. And what I will be dealing with now, as we go along, will more or less reflect what was agreed upon or what was discussed yesterday, and I would, of course, add over that and try to develop some issues, the discussion on some issues, further. When we met on the 4th of April, I had hoped at the time that the Prosecution -- that the motions, responses and replies filed in relation to the joint amended indictment would have been decided within relatively short time. I was wrong. I mean, we encountered several problems, legal problems, which we needed to address and when the cake was almost baked and ready for consumption, then I was informed that there would be soon a reshuffling and reconstituting -- reconstitution of Chambers and that one of the Judges in this pre-trial Chamber would be moved to another Trial Chamber, and that another judge from another Trial Chamber would be moved to this Chamber. I'm referring particularly to Judge Kwon who has replaced Judge Antonetti in my Chamber and the plan at least for the time being is, although I do not decide these things myself, but the plan is that Judge Kwon will be the second permanent judge who will sit on the trial which will start this summer. Then there will be an Ad Litem Judge, I would imagine, plus another Ad Litem Judge, who will serve as a Reserve Judge. So at that point in time, I decided to -- that it would be better if such a fundamental matter be decided by a judge who will be in the trial rather than by a judge who will not be in the trial. My anticipation is that this decision will be forthcoming, I hope by the end of next week. The situation at present is it has been seen, of course, by me, it has been seen by Judge Parker and it has been seen or it is being seen by Judge Kwon. When I have feedbacks from both, there will be a meeting between us, amongst us, and we will decide and then proceed with handing down the decision. But I wanted to put your mind at rest that it is not something that we are -- that we have shelved or that we are sleeping upon. It's something that is being very actively worked upon and within the end -- by the end of next week, I hope you will note the outcome of your motions. There is also another matter that, again, was prepared, ready for filing, another decision, relating to the motion by you, Madam, requesting translation of pre-trial brief, and also time for the accused, et cetera, you know what I'm talking about. I'm also referring to the other motion which you filed on the 28th of March requesting a translation into B/C/S of two other motions. And also time for your client, after the translation has been provided, to submit their responses. In case some of the accused don't know, both motions have been joined by a number of other accused; not all. The Chamber is about to hand down a decision on all these motions. It was elaborated, it has been elaborated for quite sometime. It has been seen by Judge Parker; it has also been seen by Judge Kwon. There is just one minor issue that needs to be resolved, which, in my mind, does not even require a meeting between the Judges because it can be easily resolved. And again, I can assure you that next week, this decision will be handed down. It will cover the multitude of motions that deal with the matter. There is an outstanding motion from you, Mr. Pandurevic, in which you renew your request for provisional release. I know also that you filed subsequently a second motion asking for an oral hearing. Again, this matter will -- has been actively discussed and will be decided shortly. First, obviously, everything depends on whether we grant your second motion that we have an oral hearing on the matters that you raise in it. If that is the case, first there will be the oral hearing and then eventually the judgement based on also on what emerges from that oral hearing. If there is no oral hearing, we are in a position to proceed with the decision almost forthwith. And that basically deals with your motions. Then, Mr. Pandurevic -- then there is a motion by the accused -- by Mr. Gvero for access to confidential material in the Milosevic case. This was filed on the 31st of March. Accused Pandurevic and Borovcanin have joined in, have associated themselves with that motion. This matter, I have not yet had time to discuss with the other two judges, Judge Parker and the new-comer, Judge Kwon. I will do so at the earliest opportunity and will decide it. Most importantly, in case some of you are not aware of that, on the 4th of May - that's not long ago - the Prosecution filed a motion for referral of Mr. Trbic's case to Bosnia, pursuant to Rule 11 bis. This matter has been referred by the president of the Tribunal, President Pocar, to the Referral Bench, and so it's not a matter that I, as Pre-Trial Judge, or the pre-trial Chamber will be dealing with. Of course, pending a decision on that matter, on that issue, by the Referral Bench, we will be proceeding on all other -- on all other matters. In fact we are proceeding today with this Status Conference, and the pending motions will be decided irrespective of that referral motion. Then we had a significant development anticipated, of course, because we dealt with it on the 4th of April; namely, when the Prosecution a few days ago, on the 5th of May, filed their motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts. You will recall that on the 4th of May we had agreed, or I had indicated rather than you had agreed, that counsel for the Defence will be required to file their responses within one month after the decision on the form of the indictment is issued. Since that is not yet issued, the term of one month has not yet started running. I wanted to make that clear. I do, however, invite you to start engaging yourself actively on that motion. It is an extremely important motion and we will need to decide upon it at the earliest opportunity after you have filed your responses. Then, you must be aware that barely a week ago, on the 12th of May, the Prosecution filed a motion for admission of 92 bis statements, which are also first subject to responses by the Defence. The agreement or my commitment with you is, and remains, that you will be required to file these -- your respective responses within one month after we have handed down our decision on the form of the indictment. So to my knowledge, there may be one or more documents that have arrived today. I was busy drafting the Oric judgement with the other two judges. I haven't had time to really go through them but my secretary brought in definitely something related to this case by way of motions. Yes. I come to disclosure matters. Mr. Von Hebel has informed me fully of what was discussed, what went on, yesterday in the meeting that he presided over with you, together with you. And without the need of repeating, telling you what happened yesterday, because you know, I have been invited or it has been suggested to me to turn my attention to you, Prosecution, and inquire about the exact overview of the missing -- what appears to be missing elements in the disclosure of the entire collection of Rule 66(A)(ii) statements. I understand that it's not yet completed. What I'm interested in is not details. What I'm interested in is a rough indication what the problem is so that I can then decide whether to give you a time limit within which to complete this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. During the course of preparing the Prosecution's 92 bis motion, we discovered that there were numerous statements which had not been provided either in English or in B/C/S, one or the other, but I don't believe in any case both, to the Defence counsel. In part, that was also initiate the by a meeting we had with Mr. Bourgon and Madam Nikolic regarding some specific statements they had requested. The combination of both those efforts revealed to us that we have approximately 34 statements that need to be either translated or transcribed, either into B/C/S or English. A couple of those witnesses, Your Honour, may not be on our witness list. I need to double-check that. But I would say it's approximately 30 witnesses in total. As I said in those cases, one form of the statement is disclosed, we need to disclose the other form. Obviously it's the B/C/S which is needed. What we have done, Your Honour, is prevailed upon our investigative teams and drawn language assistants from other investigative teams to assist us in expediting those reviews. We, as recently as yesterday, and Your Honour referred to the filing by the Prosecution, disclosed five witness statements in redacted form. We have prioritised the request from the Nikolic team in order to transcribe and furnish those statements as soon as possible. In terms of an actual estimate, Your Honour, I would have to consult with our deputy investigative team leader, Mr. Bob Reid, who I believe was spearheading the acquisition and devotion of those assets to transcribing those statements. But I can tell you that we are working full speed with every resource that we have in our office to get those done. That has been something we have been working on for a solid week now in terms of drawing on those investigative team language assistants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Is there anyone from the various Defence teams that would like to address this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have initiated two meetings, and we have considered the report that the honourable Chamber has received from our colleagues, but there are more than 30 witnesses involved. And the redacted statements by the protected witnesses we received only yesterday and only in English, and they do relate to specific events and the responsibility of the accused in certain events. This slows down our investigation and this is what raises concern, and that is why we would like to speed up the process of the disclosure of those statements that we are still missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I perfectly agree with you, Madam Nikolic, not only for the reasons that you mentioned but also for the fact that we need to move. I was thinking of two, maximum three, weeks in which to complete this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, without consulting, that sounds to me a reasonable period of time in which to complete that project. And if, at any point, it looks like we will not be able to meet that, we will advise the Court and perhaps there are other resources of which we may avail ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So it's been decided to fix a time limit of three weeks from today within which to complete the disclosure exercise, first of Rule 66(A)(ii) statements. And I move to Rule 68 disclosure. I understand that there has been some kind of misunderstanding in relation to the hard disk containing -- external hard disk containing Rule 68 material that we talked about during the 4th April Status Conference. I only became aware of it after the yesterday's 65 ter meeting, and, of course, I am offering you both my help here to solve the problem, if there is a problem, and expedite the solution, because I am sure that a solution is needed in any case. So as I take it, it is that initially, it was not understood that there was going to be only one external hard disk that would do the complete round from Defence team to Defence team. That's, I think, what is the source of the problem. What is the actual problem is that, at least at the end of the 65 ter meeting, it wasn't apparent, it wasn't known, who had -- who is in possession at this time or at that time of the external hard disk, and we need to find that first and then I think from then onwards a solution is easy. Does any one of the Defence team -- is anyone from the Defence team in a position to provide the relative information?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's good. I take it, and without having to go through all this, that I think you are all aware now that this needs to do the round. I take it also that some of the teams have already gone through this process. It has been available to some of you. Whoever has this external disk, please, sits down with the rest of you who haven't had the opportunity to make use of it, and try to solve it this way. All right? I am not going to address this matter any further. I know that you will deal with it amongst yourselves. Okay? But, of course, it is my duty to inquire whether you have any other disclosure worries or concerns. I see none. There are no other disclosure that you are aware of from the Prosecution side?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Usually I would discuss with you the matter of agreed facts, but I think it's too premature to do that, also because we haven't handed down our decision on the motions that I mentioned. That will come later. But needless to say, I keep this completely separate and distinct from the merit of the Prosecution motion in relation to adjudicated facts. It has got nothing to do with that. It's a completely separate notion. Now, can we go a little bit for sometime in private session, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Ram. Let's now deal with the most important part of -- or almost the most important part of this Status Conference, and that is the work plan. I want you to know that I am completely aware of the problems that you both have in relation to the starting of the -- and proceeding of this trial. And it is certainly not my intention to disregard them. In fact, I have discussed them with Mr. Von Hebel yesterday, and I have been thinking about them, and as far as I can, I will try to accommodate everyone. I also wish to make things clear, that the completion strategy has got nothing to do -- it's not in the back of my mind, only except in so far as the longer it takes to start this trial, the longer other trials will -- other accused and other trials will have to wait, and the greater will be the risks for everyone that justice will not be done. So my concerns about the completion strategy is only in relation that it -- I take upon myself that it is my duty to ensure that we start this trial and that possibly we could start all other trials and bring them to an end as early as we can. On the other hand, I also have problems of my own. I am at the moment involved in the drafting of the Oric final judgement, and my anticipation is that the final judgement will be handed down at the end -– the last day of June, plus or minus -- not minus, maybe plus one or two days, if needs be. And that's unless I encounter, together with my other two judges, major problems, which has been the case sometimes, not -- not in the Oric case only, but in every other case. So that's the schedule. As I explained to you earlier, one of the other judges in the trial will be a permanent Judge. The other two will be Ad Litem Judges. There is no way Ad Litem Judges and no sense in appointing Ad Litem Judges, bringing them over and swearing them in during the summer recess when no one is here. On the other hand, bringing them over after the summer recess, that's the second week of August, would mean that there is no way that we can start the trial any time soon because they would have to settle down and also familiarise themselves with a case which is not a minor case. I know how much work is involved in preparing for this trial. So my idea is to have the Ad Litem Judge and the Reserve Judge here in time to be able to be in a position then to start the trial with me and Judge Kwon fully -- fully instructed or fully informed about what needs to be done, about the facts of this case, before we start trial. So what is my proposition or my plan, at least for the moment, and again I mean there are ifs and buts and anything could happen which might change this schedule that I have in mind. My idea is that we need to come in the courtroom and start the trial before the recess, because that would give me the opportunity and the possibility of having the Ad Litem Judges here in the beginning of July. And I would be able to sit with them and discuss with them and prepare the beginning -- the start of the trial. I'm talking of having a Pre-Trial Conference on the 13th of July, and, of course, for that trial conference, Pre-Trial Conference, there will be the Ad Litem Judge and the Reserve Judge. Then, on the day after, on the 14th of July, we will have the official opening of the trial. Nothing special will happen that day, because I understand that there are problems from the Prosecution's side but also from the Defence side. The period of the recess will serve all of us to instruct ourselves better and to be prepared then to start first with the opening statements and order. However, I understand that because of what we discussed and the indication that I gave during the 4th April Status Conference, some of you, both from the Prosecution side and from the Defence side, have entered into commitments which, at least on the advice of my Senior Legal Officer, make it pretty much impossible to have the opening statements on the part -- by the Prosecution before the 20th of August. So my idea is that there are, and will still be, several very important household matters to deal with, which will be dealt, as necessary, during the preceding week, that is, the week starting on the 14th of August. You will be advised beforehand what these household matters will be, because much depends on what happens between now, the next Status Conference, the Pre-Trial Conference, and so on and so forth. So it could well be that one of those days or more will be dedicated to the matter that we discussed in private session. It could well be other matters. I am not in a position to anticipate what or which at the present moment, but the idea is that that week will be dedicated to resolving all the issues that need to be resolved before we really start the trial. This is the proposition that I am making and the plan that I have in my mind. At the same time, it would accommodate all those who have had these prior commitments which may be difficult now to move. And then we take it up basically from the 21st of August onwards, when I understand the Prosecution will be in a position to make its opening statements. In the meantime, I would appreciate very much if, maybe too early now, but if in due course and by the time of the Pre-Trial Conference in July, you give us an indication whether it is your intention -- I mean any one of the teams -- to make opening statements too, and whether you are in a position to advise the Trial Chamber if any of your respective clients will be making statements as they are entitled to do. Any such statements, of course, will follow the opening statements of the Prosecutor. I barely need to state that. All right? As I said, this is all tentative. The whole schedule can shift depending on various contingencies. Anything could happen. You might even have difficulties in finding Ad Litem Judges, for example, who can come at such short notice. So we will play it by the ear. I will do my utmost to try and schedule the start of the trial and the continuation of the trial in a way which would not create any problems for any one of you; at the same time trying to make sure that we are in a position then when we start to continue without major hurdles. Are there any comments that you would like to make on this before I proceed further on other matters, related matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From the Defence? Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Your Honour. At this moment, could we be advised of the date of the next Status Conference and the next 65 ter meeting? This would help us with our work on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Nikolic, this has been on my mind, and it has been on my mind because it's not difficult for me to say that the next Status Conference will be on such and such a day. The situation as it is now has changed dramatically, in the sense that there is now a permanent Judge, Judge Kwon, who is not involved in any other trial at the moment, who will be the second permanent Judge in this trial, who will also be dealing with several matters. So progress can be accelerated, to a large extent. The problem that I have is you -- I mean, when I say "you" I mean all of you, because I know that you are not all permanently residing here at all times; some of you are, some of you aren't. Some of you have to travel. And so this is the problem that I have. And those of you who are not here, I would take it for granted are not sitting pretty doing nothing at home. So my problem is I would like to have another Status Conference, not later than a month, not later, much later, than after the expiration of the month that you have for the filing of your response on the Prosecution motion on the adjudicated facts, on the filing on other matters that I mentioned earlier. The month will start running presumably from the end of next month. I am pretty sure that either way we decide these issues, there is -- there probably will be an appeal, if not on all motions, at least on one, on one decision. But still, I think my plan is that soon after the expiration of that month, when we have in front of us your filings and we can roughly gauge where we are, then there will be another Status Conference, preceded by a 65 ter meeting. We are talking, hopefully, if I hand down those decisions next week, we are talking of a Status Conference which would probably be convened the end of June, end of June, more or less the last few days of June. If I have problems with the Oric case, that could be moved to the first week of July. But I would anticipate that in preparation of the Pre- Trial Conference that will take place in July in any case, that you would try to make an effort to be here more or less the last -- the end part of June, beginning of July, for a Status Conference, 65 ter meeting, Status Conference, and subsequently but soon after, for the Pre-Trial Conference. That's what I have in mind. I don't think there is any point in organising another Status Conference between now and when you file your responses to the Prosecution, pending the Prosecution motions that I mentioned earlier, unless there are serious and urgent matters that need to be addressed, in which case we will follow the same procedure as in the past. You will -- the SLO will communicate with you and see -- and try to organise a day, set a day which is convenient to everyone. That's my plan, all right? Thank you for bringing that up, Madam Nikolic, because it was important. Now, I asked the Senior Legal Officer, Mr. Von Hebel, yesterday, to discuss with you, and more or less find out your reaction to, the system that was adopted in Prlic, in the Prlic case, during the final stages of the pre-trial phase, which required the Prosecution to file in XL format all the relative details in relation to evidence as it relates to counts, witnesses as they relate to counts and events, and documentation and everything. I have been given to understand that the association of Defence counsel looks very favourably on that form of presenting the Prosecution case prior to the commencement of the trial. I'm given the information that it is a very valuable kind of document for the Trial Chamber and for the parties to have, as it would enable the Trial Chamber then to be -- pre-trial Chamber to be actively involved with the Prosecution in establishing time limit for the conclusion of the Prosecution -- for the presentation and conclusion of the Prosecution case and also the kind of evidence that really needs to be brought forward. I take it that you were informed of this yesterday, that I look favourably on this system of approaching the Prosecution pre-trial brief for the purpose of preparing trial. And unless I hear serious objections from the Defence that would convince me to the contrary, or of the contrary, it is my plan to fix a time limit for the Prosecution, with a clear indication that this would be the procedure to follow in preparation of the case, or in preparation of the trial. Can I have a feedback from the Prosecution on this and then, of course, I will turn on the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Candidly, we have not had an opportunity to discuss the Prlic decision with respect to that specific issue of the XL format. I can tell you that we will continue to do everything we can to make the evidence available in the most efficient and effective manner for all parties involved, but unfortunately I cannot provide an answer to the Court at this point as to whether we will be capable of delivering upon that promise, were we to make that promise with respect to the spread sheets. We have just furnished our exhibit list; we may have some additional exhibits to add to that. So we ourselves are in that process, and I will endeavour to provide the Court with an answer once we delve a little more deeply into that. Unfortunately, that's the best answer I can give you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. On the other hand, I know at firsthand although initially there was some resistance on the part of the Prosecution in that case, the ultimate conclusion is that it's something that actually facilitates your labours, and that it should be the system or the method that should be adopted. That's from the Prosecution side. I think if you inquire further, you would be able to confirm what I am telling you. From the Defence side, is there -- it concerns you very little, actually, because I'm sure it will give you more information and more organised information, but is there anyone who would like to contribute to this debate or show any concerns about this? My idea is that this will not delay the progress of the preparations for trial. Rather, it would instruct the preparatory stage much better and instruct you much better. But if there are any concerns, I would be very pleased to hear them. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I would just like to say a quick remark, not specifically related to a what you just mentioned but to something that my colleague from the Prosecution just mentioned. Maybe I misunderstood, but he said we have just completed our list of exhibits. My understanding is that the list of exhibits was given to us with the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, and the reason I mention this at this point is that we would like to avoid receiving additional material that we are not aware of at this time between now and the start of the trial. And again, this is important because, specifically for the client that we represent, most of the evidence that has been given to us by the Prosecution, and the Prosecution has yet to give to us, as was candidly admitted by my colleague, dates from, very often, January of 2006, and we are wondering what is happening here, because this case has been going on for quite some time. The Prosecution has been working on this case for more than ten years, and suddenly we see these statements being collected in, let's say, November, December 2005, January 2006. Now, maybe we have additional exhibits being prepared. We just would like to know the case we have to meet, and for this we need to have some kind of certainty with respect to the witnesses that will be called by the Prosecution and with respect to the exhibits that they will use. To this day, we take it for granted that we are working on the basis of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, and we would like Your Honour, the Chamber, to be quite firm, in that if there are any changes to that list, to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, that they should justify why they have not been able to come up with exactly what is the case against the client we represent up to this time. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'm sure that the officer, prosecuting officer knows exactly what you're talking about, what the problem -- what his responsibilities are. I will not involve myself in this, because obviously, as you put it, this could be a matter contested between you and I would have to decide it. So I'm keeping my distance. Of course, if you would like to remark on --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may briefly, Your Honour. Just to put Mr. Bourgon's mind somewhat at ease, I was referring to our 65 ter exhibit list when I referred to our recent exhibit list. There is not another separate list that we are going to spring on Defence counsel. We do, however, as I mentioned, have some handful of additional exhibits, which we will provide probably on CD format once we have compiled that list. The reason why, in shortest terms, that some of these statements have not been made available sooner is that these interviews, as Mr. Bourgon noted, were conducted in January of 2006. The reason why some of this investigation has been done or conducted at that point is we have been meeting better success with cooperation among some of these witnesses. It is simply a product of the timing. But we will endeavour, as we have been on a number of issues that I won't burden the Court with, in a one-on-one relationship with Defence counsel, to resolve these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that information. Last but not least on this -- on the matter of the trial, I will need definitely, before the trial starts, or as soon as it starts, to give you a deadline by which time period -- time period by which you have to conclude your case, and I will be doing the same with you. So this is a matter that you need to start addressing. Now, your position is much more clear than the position of the Defence because in the case of the Defence, there is always that element of uncertainty, not knowing exactly what evidence will be produced here in the courtroom. I am also fully aware that in trying to fix the time limit for the Prosecution case, the question of Rule 92 bis evidence assumes a great importance. This is why it will be necessary for me, after the expiration of the month following the decision on the form of the indictment, that I will come back to you. At that point in time, at that point in time, I would know more or less where you stand in relation to the motion of the Prosecution relating to 92 bis evidence, and that would help me come to a conclusion. But you also should start thinking, as from now, the several Defence teams, about an estimate of time you require for presenting your own Defence case, because I would need to know that, and short of any information I would still have to fix a time limit in any case. So that's the position. I think I have made myself clear on this. Is there anyone of you that would like to raise any other matter in relation to the trial itself, trial matters? I see none, which brings me to the next matter. Is there anything else that you would like to raise before I address the eight accused here and ask them about their health situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Nothing from the Defence? I see none. Thank you. So I will go through the whole process as in previous Status Conferences. Before I do so, however, there is one final thing that I need to address to you, Mr. Borovcanin and your counsel, Mr. Lazarevic. You will recall that last time there was this issue about whether you should or shouldn't enter a plea or whether you weren't -- were prepared to enter a plea to one of the counts that you had. And we had agreed that since that was a matter that was the subject matter of one of the pending motions, I would be dealing with that and then eventually you would be given the opportunity either to enter a plea or not to enter a plea, in which case I would enter a plea on your behalf. The matter is going to be decided. It's part of the decision that I referred to earlier on, which I will be handing down hopefully next week, so I'm not asking you to enter any plea today. That will come next time. And the same reservation, Madam Fauveau and also Mr. Krgovic, there is still the matter of your clients having to enter a plea. We will come to that. There is no point in bringing them over to enter a plea or make a video connection there and make them enter a plea now. That can be done later on. So, Mr. Popovic, would you like to raise any matter relating to your state of health or condition of detention? We are in open session. If it is your preference that if there is anything to discuss that would you like to discuss it in closed session or in private session, then we will go into private or closed session. THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] No need for us to go into private session, Your Honour. But I do have some comments and objections that are relative to the work of Mr. Jovanovic, the way he collects information and deals with the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. The transcript says "Mr. Jovanovic". You mean Mr. -- your council, Mr. Zoran Zivanovic? THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wanted to make sure, because if you're out of it, you're out of it; but if you are in, you are in. Who are you referring to? THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] I'm referring to Mr. Jovanovic who works for the Registry and who has to do with the financial situation of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. All right. And so what is your problem? What is your complaint? THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] My concern has to do with the way he does what he does. When he spoke to my wife in Belgrade, he told her that we have everything provided for us here. And I am a diabetic and I need different types of food, as a result of which I have increased expenses. I receive food as any other detainee, which shouldn't be the case. I've already written complaints about that. Second of all, with regard to the fact that he said that we have everything provided to us, I claim that that is not the fact. There are some things missing by way of clothes and other things that we have to purchase ourselves. The allocation that he came up with, I don't know how he did that, according to which rule, and how he came to the conclusion that some of the Defence has to be paid for and some of it doesn't have to be paid for, I believe that this is not realistic and it does not rely on facts. Whoever makes such a decision has to reconsider and has to come up with a realistic financial base, because what he's doing now is disgraceful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Popovic. Let's take things one by one. The decisions of the Registrar relating to financial matters, et cetera, are dealt with by the various directives and regulations and -- that we have, and the accused has always got a remedy that can be explored. I am sure that if you discuss this with Mr. Zivanovic, he will explain the whole process. The Trial Chamber does not get involved in that unless - unless - the conclusions reached by the Registrar are unreasonable, not based on the facts that he has in front of him, or when they are so grievous, so serious, that they may or do influence on your right to have a fair trial. That's when we get involved. And we have been involved in the past, both in relation to when the Registrar decides that you need to pay part of your legal costs, but again our jurisdiction there is limited. The other matter that you raised -- so I suggest that you discuss that with Mr. Zivanovic. However, I will be copying that part and communicating it to the Registrar so that if he needs -- or feels that he needs to act upon it, he will do so. And I have, believe me, I say it publicly, I have full trust in the Registrar, that he will do his duty. And if he doesn't, then we intervene, and we have intervened in the past. I mean, I have reversed decisions taken by the Registrar, even in relation to the matters that I am talking about. The other matter about diabetes, yes, it is of concern to me. Are you receiving medical treatment in the Detention Unit for your diabetic condition or not? Do you have diabetes 1 or diabetes 2, to start with? THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] To be honest I don't know if it's 1 or 2. I receive one tablet in the morning, one 500 milligram tablet in the morning, and that is that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have diabetes type 2 and not type 1, because otherwise you would be receiving insulin. That's why I asked you what the situation -- what the situation is. What I am going to do is that I will also copy this part of your statement to the commandant of the Detention Unit, Mr. McFadden, and if necessary discuss the matter -- discuss the matter with him. I have no doubt in my mind that if you have a diabetic condition, you shouldn't be eating everything that everyone else is eating. So that's definitely something that I will interest myself in, and the Registrar has taken note of what I have said. I think the entire statement of the accused, plus my intervention, needs to be blocked, copied, to the Registrar, and the first part of his statement relating to his diabetic condition needs to be copied, together with the latter part of my intervention, to Mr. Tim McFadden, with direction, a direction to -- direct to Mr. McFadden to make his remarks. It's not an option. He has to make his remarks to the Trial Chamber on the accused's complaint, and any other matter related thereto, within a week from service -- within a week from service, of the communication. Did you get me, Ram?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's been noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the matter of diabetes has been -- THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Popovic. THE ACCUSED POPOVIC: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that I don't want to be misunderstood. In the Detention Unit I have increased expenses which Mr. Jovanovic did not want to admit. I buy my own fruit; I buy my own sweeteners. He knows that, but he's reluctant to admit that. That's why I have made you aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. As I said, that's also very important and it will be communicated to the Registrar, and communicating it to the Registrar, I would expect also the Registrar to come back to me and tell me what his position is on all this. But I also want -- would like you to discuss the matter with your counsel, because there are remedies that are provided for in the rules or the regulations of this Tribunal and you should first exhaust those remedies before involving the Trial Chamber. But I will definitely involve myself in both matters, to the extent that I can. Mr. Beara? My same question to you. Do you have any comments, complaints or remarks on your state of health or detention? THE ACCUSED BEARA: [Interpretation] No, I have no objections at all. Everything is in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Beara. Mr. Nikolic? Same question to you. THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have any complaints. There are some minor matters that I might be complaining of, but I'm dealing with those with my lawyers. My health condition is good and everything else is good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin? Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have any particular comment or complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The microphone wasn't switched on. Thank you. But I still see that it has come on the transcript. I thank the interpreters for pointing that out and for entering the accused's statement in any case. So Mr. Pandurevic? Same question. THE ACCUSED PANDUREVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as my health is concerned, and as far as my detention conditions are concerned, I don't have any complaints. But I would like to raise my concern about the materials and whether we will be able to receive them in a language that we understand. So far we only have the pre-trial brief in English, which we don't understand, and we would very much like to get it in our own language well in advance of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Pandurevic. As you must have heard me before, that is a matter that is going to be decided next week, not only in relation to the pre-trial brief but also in relation to other documents and motions. Last, Mr. Trbic. Same question to you. Any complaints about your state of health or state of detention? THE ACCUSED TRBIC: [Interpretation] As far as the Detention Unit and my health, I have no complaints. I would just like to convey to you that there has been a hearsay about the transfer of my case to Sarajevo, to Bosnia, that is. I would like to address to you with a request, if possible, that there should be no more talk about that until I'm appointed a new lawyer, which I believe will be done next week. And, of course, I need a certain time with my new lawyer to prepare for any possible discussion on my transfer to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Trbic. As I stated earlier on, that is a matter with which I will not be dealing and the pre-trial Chamber will not be dealing, so you will not have to worry about that, as far as the pre-trial Chamber is concerned. I mean, you will have all the opportunity, you and your new counsel, to make your submissions to the Referral Bench that will be deciding on that issue. It's not me or my Trial Chamber that will be dealing with it. It's another Chamber, another team of judges. But one of the pre-trial judges, that's Judge Parker, will be on the Referral Bench, will be on the Referral Bench, so that's the position. And the decision of the Trial Chamber, then, obviously will depend on what will be the outcome of the referral case, which brings me to a completely different topic related to one that we discussed earlier on, included in the ifs and buts, because one of the developments is precisely this motion by the Prosecution to have Mr. Trbic referred -- to be tried in Bosnia, with the consequence that there would be -- his case would be severed from that of the rest of you. If the matter is not yet decided by the referral court by the time we are supposed to start, unless there is a specific, separate motion to have the accused Trbic separated, severed, from the rest, that would be another problem that we will have in front of us, and it could well end up with being a critical matter for the Trial Chamber to decide, possibly also delaying the start of the trial. But again, please do understand that I am in the same predicament as you are, and the ifs and buts, if you have ifs and buts, I have got more of them than you do, and I will try to deal with what arises accordingly. So I think we have covered what we needed to cover. I do wish to publicly thank you for your cooperation, not only today but also in the interval between Status Conferences. My Senior Legal Officer keeps me informed of every single bit of development and how productive and how cooperative his interactions with you are. I do appreciate that because it makes things easier for me and the Trial Chamber, and I can assure you of my cooperation, full cooperation, in return. As agreed, please plan for another Status Conference at the end of June or, latest, beginning of July, and then to be followed with a Pre- Trial Conference, unless we have a cataclysm that would require postponement or rescheduling of everything. Thank you and good afternoon to everybody.

procedural_notes.text: [The accused Miletic and Gvero not present]
--- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
